title: The paper's headline long-run claim — automation implies job consolidation — is never proved and is false in the model's own algebra
location: 5_longrun.tex, Sec 5.3 ("Hand-off Costs and the Limits of Worker Specialization"), paragraph beginning "AI moves this balance..."; echoed in 1_introduction.tex l.15 and in the title "Redefining Work"
claim: Section 5.3 asserts: "A chain replaces a run of steps with a single verification at its endpoint, so it strips out the skills the automated steps used to demand... That lowers the wage rate a bundled job must pay, and with it the penalty from bundling... With a fixed set of production steps, this means that one worker's job extends to absorb the tasks of adjacent workers. Automation and job consolidation are therefore two sides of the same coin in our framework, which is the sense in which AI also redefines work rather than merely displacing it from a fixed set of jobs." No proposition, lemma, or proof supports this. Grep confirms the only \begin{proposition} environments in the paper are in 4_implications.tex (Props 1-2, short run) and 6_extensions.tex (Props 3-4, algorithms). Section 5 contains zero formal results. And the claim is false. Take two tasks, so h_2 = 0 by the paper's own convention h_m = 0. From eq (7): merging beats splitting iff sigma_1*h_1 > sigma_1*t_2 + sigma_2*t_1. Because the hand-off time h_1 enters (10) multiplied by the *handing-off* job's skill, AI that lowers sigma_1 shrinks the benefit of merging exactly as fast as it shrinks its cost, and the residual term sigma_2*t_1 does not shrink at all. Concrete counterexample: task 1 manual (sigma=4, t=2) or AI-chained (sigma=0.8, t=1); task 2 manual (sigma=1, t=2); h_1 = 3, h_2 = 0. Pre-AI: merged costs (4+1)(2+2) = 20, split costs 4(3+2) + 1(2) = 22, so the firm bundles. Post-AI (the firm adopts AI on task 1 since both its skill and its time fall): merged costs (0.8+1)(1+2) = 5.4, split costs 0.8(3+1) + 1(2) = 5.2, so the firm now *splits*. AI adoption fragments the job rather than consolidating it, with hand-off costs held fixed.
why_it_matters: This is the entire economic content of Section 5 and one half of the paper's title. If the claim is unproved and admits counterexamples, Section 5 delivers no result at all: it is a two-force verbal trade-off, a geometric picture, and a hand-picked 3-task numerical example (Table D.1) in which the AI strategy is *held fixed* ("under a fixed AI deployment strategy T"), so the example never exhibits the comparative static being claimed. A ReStud referee who spends ten minutes with eq (10) will find this, and the finding is not repairable by adding caveats: the sign of dJ/d(alpha) genuinely depends on *which* job in the chain gets the skill reduction, which the paper never notices.
already_addressed: Section 5.3 does discuss a force pushing the other way, but attributes it exclusively to a channel *outside* the model: "Working in the opposite direction, we treat hand-off costs as fixed, whereas AI plausibly lowers them too, by absorbing the peripheral coordination work of a transfer... The net effect of AI on job breadth is therefore an empirical question our framework poses rather than settles." That concession is about h_i falling. It does not cover the counterexample above, in which h_i is fixed and the reversal comes from the model's own multiplicative wage bill. Appendix D (app:jobdesign_example) reports the 3-task costs but holds the AI strategy fixed. A.3 (non-monotonicity) is short-run only: it works with C_T(alpha) = K_T + sum a_r alpha^{-D_c}, which contains no skill and no job design.
fix: State and prove a proposition. The natural one: give necessary and sufficient conditions on (sigma^M, sigma^A, m, a, d, h) under which the optimal job design coarsens in the refinement order as alpha rises, and show by example that it fails otherwise. Given the paper's own Section 4.3 non-monotonicity result and the fact that Prop 4 has to settle for a (1+eps)-approximation, a clean monotone comparative static may well be unavailable, in which case the honest result is a characterization of when consolidation versus fragmentation occurs — which would be a genuinely interesting theorem and would give Section 5 a reason to exist.

title: Appendix B does not derive a CES aggregate; it assumes one and reverse-engineers the firm distribution, using a derivation that is internally inconsistent because the "constants" it differentiates through are functions of the differentiation variable
location: B_macro_production.tex, Sec B.2 ("Cross-Firm Aggregation") and B.3 ("Derivation of the Effective AI Quality Heterogeneity Distribution"); the skill-adjusted time definition in Sec B (eq. skill_adjusted_time); abstract of 0_main.tex
claim: The appendix states the method plainly: "This requires either determining the macro production function parameters from the distribution of heterogeneity, or specifying the form of heterogeneity given a set of macro production function parameters. We adopt the latter approach and derive the output probability density function in terms of effective AI quality, denoted phi(alpha-bar), as a function of theta_A, theta_M, rho." So (B.10) is posited, not derived, and (B.13) is the unique density that makes the posited form hold. That is a knife-edge existence statement, not a micro-foundation. Worse, the derivation is invalid on its own terms. It defines u = w_A*T_A/(1 - w_M*T_M), forms the identity (B.14), and differentiates with respect to u treating T_A and T_M as constants. But T_A and T_M are, by the appendix's own definition, functions of w_A and w_M: the skill-adjusted time of task b is [w_M*sum(sigma^M) + w_A*sum(sigma^A)]/w_{E(b)} * t_b, aggregated in (B.7)-(B.8). Moreover the appendix has already stipulated that T and J solve the firm's cost-minimization problem (7), whose solution depends on w_A and w_M. Tracing out the aggregate isoquant necessarily means varying relative wages, and every object held fixed in the ODE moves when they do. Levhari's original argument is legitimate because his micro input coefficients are technological primitives; here they are endogenous outcomes of the paper's own optimization.
why_it_matters: The abstract advertises this as a result: "and show that firm-level production aggregates to a macroeconomic CES production function." What is actually shown is that IF a particular wage-and-organization-dependent density holds, THEN a CES identity can be made to hold locally, via a derivation that is not valid. A referee who checks the derivation will conclude the paper's one macro claim is wrong, and abstract-level overclaims are expensive. Separately, the objects are not well-defined: "A firm with effective AI quality alpha-bar thus produces output x = phi(alpha-bar) by definition" equates a firm's output *level* to a *density* value, which is dimensionally incoherent; and phi in (B.13) is never shown to be non-negative, never shown to integrate to at most the unit mass of firms, and never checked against the capacity constraint implied by the appendix's own normalization ("exactly one unit of capital is required per unit of output" plus fixed firm capital implies x <= 1 for every firm).
already_addressed: Section 6.1 flags the assumptions in a footnote: "The representation asks more of the economy than the firm-level argument does: capital productivity is common across firms, every firm organizes identically, and realized effective AI quality is the single dimension along which firms differ," and the body notes the Houthakker-Levhari composition mechanism. That footnote lists the *auxiliary* assumptions. It does not disclose that the CES functional form is itself assumed and the distribution backed out of it, and it does not touch the T_A/T_M-versus-u inconsistency, which appears nowhere in the paper. Grep of B.3 confirms T_A and T_M are treated as constants throughout the differentiation.
fix: Either (i) restate the result honestly as "there exists a distribution of effective AI quality under which the aggregate is CES" (a Levhari-style existence result), prove that (B.13) is a valid density on [u,1] for a non-empty parameter region, and repair the ODE by carrying dT_A/du and dT_M/du through it — noting explicitly that firms' T and J re-optimize as wages move; or (ii) go the other way: fix a primitive distribution of AI ability (Pareto, say), and characterize the aggregate elasticity of substitution it generates, showing how it depends on the *chaining* structure. Option (ii) would actually make the appendix earn its place. Failing both, cut Appendix B and the sentence from the abstract.

title: The wage technology — wage rate equals summed skill, wage bill equals summed skill times summed time — is asserted, is inconsistent with every standard assignment or human-capital model, and its superadditivity is the sole source of the paper's specialization force
location: 5_longrun.tex Sec 5.1, eq (5) Wage_j = sum sigma_b and eq (6)/(10) WageBill_j = (sum sigma_b)(h(J_j) + sum t_b), with the motivating footnote; B_macro_production.tex eq (B.5) and its footnote
claim: The paper writes: "We then assume that a worker's wage is proportional to the skill level of their job," and the footnote concedes the point: "One motivation for this formulation is workers paying a human capital investment to acquire the skills necessary for a job... Rather than formalizing such a wage model here, we impose this as an assumption and provide a more detailed wage formulation in Appendix B." Appendix B does not deliver on that promise: (B.5) merely attaches base rates w_M and w_A to the two skill types, and its own footnote says "This formulation is essentially equivalent to the original definition of wage in (5)." So the forward reference is empty. The substantive problem is what (6) implies. Expanding for two tasks, the wage bill of a bundled job is sigma_1*t_1 + sigma_2*t_2 + (sigma_1*t_2 + sigma_2*t_1); the paper reads the cross terms correctly — "The remainder of their human capital sits idle at that moment and is paid for regardless" — but never asks what rules out selling that idle capacity. If a worker can sell skill-hours to more than one job, or is paid per skill actually used, the cross terms vanish, bundling is costless, and Section 5's entire trade-off collapses into "specialize fully." The limit on specialization is therefore produced by an unmodeled contracting friction (a worker is indivisible and must be paid at the job's maximum skill rate for its whole duration), not by anything derived. Relatedly, skill acquisition is exactly additive across tasks — sum sigma_b, with no economies of scope in learning — which is the opposite of what the human-capital literature the footnote invokes assumes.
why_it_matters: Section 5's central object (10) has no labour-market foundation, so nothing in it is disciplined by theory or evidence. Because every worker is ex ante identical and can acquire any skill at the same cost, there is no assignment problem at all: "job design" is a partition problem, and the paper's own headline about "overturning comparative advantage" is about AI-versus-human at a step, never about worker-versus-worker. A ReStud referee will immediately ask how this relates to Rosen (1983) on the utilization rate of skill investment, to Becker-Murphy (1992) where specialization is limited by coordination *and* by the extent of the market, and above all to Garicano (2000), whose knowledge-acquisition-plus-communication-cost technology is the canonical formalization of exactly this trade-off and would deliver eq (5) or something better from primitives. Without that, Section 5 reads as a partition-cost exercise dressed in labour-economics vocabulary.
already_addressed: The literature review (2_literature.tex, "Division of Labor and the Boundary of the Job") cites murphy1986specialization, becker1992division, dessein2006adaptive and Coase-Williamson, and mentions Garicano only inside a footnote about someone else's paper: "ide2025ai provides a related view... embedding AI as an autonomous problem solver in a knowledge hierarchy model [garicano2000hierarchies, garicano2006organization]." Sattinger, Costinot-Vogel, Rosen (1983) and Kremer's O-ring wage implications are absent from the wage discussion entirely (Kremer appears only as an analogy for step complementarity). No part of the paper compares (5)-(6) to any of these technologies or shows what the results owe to the functional form.
fix: Micro-found (5). The cleanest route: a two-period human-capital model in which a worker pays a one-time cost c(S) to acquire skill bundle S, works a fixed career, and free entry drives the wage rate to the amortized cost; then eq (5) is the special case c(S) = sum_b sigma_b and the paper can state which results survive concave c. Second, state the contracting friction that prevents skill-hours from being sold separately, and show the specialization trade-off is a consequence of it, not an assumption alongside it. Third, at minimum, show whether Section 5's conclusions survive sub-additive skill acquisition — since with sufficient scope economies in learning the bundling penalty vanishes and the interior optimum disappears.

title: There is no equilibrium object anywhere in the paper: wages, the exit margin, and the return to capital are all free parameters or residuals, and the appendix's "free entry" and "equilibrium" language is not backed by any market-clearing condition
location: 5_longrun.tex l.5; B_macro_production.tex Sec B.2 (profitability condition, threshold eq. alpha_threshold, and the footnote assuming a parameter range for w_A, w_M, T_A, T_M)
claim: Section 5 opens: "Free entry in the labor market also lets it pay workers according to the actual skill requirements of the jobs it designs, rather than at the rate the short run held fixed." No entry margin, no worker participation constraint, no labour supply and no market clearing for the two labour types is written down anywhere; grep for "equilibrium", "market clear", "labor supply" across the body returns only this sentence and three lines in Appendix B, all of which are within-firm Leontief accounting ("In equilibrium, allocation of labor to tasks satisfies x = L_1/T_1 = ..."). w_A and w_M are exogenous constants restricted only by an assumption footnote: "We assume the parameters w_A, w_M, T_A, T_M are such that 0 < (w_A*T_A)/(1 - w_M*T_M) < 1." The one selection margin in the paper, the exit threshold in (B.9), comes from a zero-profit condition w_A*L_A + w_M*L_M <= x in which capital costs nothing and is the residual claimant, so "only firms with realized effective AI quality level above this threshold will produce in equilibrium and others exit the market" is a statement about the sign of a residual, not about an equilibrium. And aggregate capital is then set to K = 1 in (B.10) even though the exiting mass of firms holds capital that is idle, so the K in the CES is not the employed capital.
why_it_matters: The paper's stated ambition is aggregate: Section 6.1 asks "how much labor the economy employs, how output responds to capital and to labor, and what becomes of both as AI improves." None of these can be answered without a wage-determination mechanism, because all of them are answers about how w_A and w_M move when alpha rises. The paper's own comparative statics run in the wrong direction: firms optimize taking w as given, aggregate labour demand shifts, and nothing sends the wage back. A general-interest theory referee's first question — what is the equilibrium object, and what is the equilibrium comparative static with respect to alpha? — currently has no answer beyond "the firm's cost falls."
already_addressed: Section 6.1 acknowledges the gap in framing ("So far we have focused on a single firm's production... What ultimately matters, however, is how these firm-level adjustments translate into the broader labor market") and offers Appendix B as the bridge. But Appendix B closes the model only on the *output* side (via the reverse-engineered phi) and leaves w_A, w_M exogenous throughout. Footnote foot:wage in Section 5 gestures at this — "different tasks T_b within job J_j could have different base wage rates w_b that could be influenced, for example, by the supply of and demand for labor of the corresponding type" — and then normalizes them to 1. So the paper knows the issue exists and defers it everywhere.
fix: Close the labour market. Fix inelastic (or elastic) supplies of the two labour types, let firms' optimal T and J generate demands, and solve for (w_A, w_M) that clear both markets. Then do the comparative static that the paper actually cares about: how do w_A/w_M, the AI-management labour share, and average job breadth respond to a rise in alpha, once wages adjust? That is the paper's missing result, and it would also repair Findings 1 and 2, since equilibrium wages are exactly what the Appendix B derivation needs to vary coherently.

title: Hand-off costs are undisciplined primitives whose formalization contradicts the story told for them, and Section 5 is therefore untestable by construction — even though the paper already has the data needed to measure them
location: 5_longrun.tex Sec 5.1 (hand-off paragraphs and the definition h(J_j) = h_i, h_m = 0) and eq (10); 7_empirics.tex l.4; H_external_validation.tex Sec H.2 (4TU event logs)
claim: The motivation is explicitly about the receiver reconstructing accumulated context: "whoever receives it has to be told what was done, why, and what state the output is now in" and "Others fall in the middle of something, where whoever receives the work has to reconstruct the context the previous worker had built up." The formalization matches none of it. (i) Only the sender's time is charged: "we write h_i for the additional hand-off time spent by a worker for whom the last step of their job is s_i"; the receiver pays nothing. (ii) h_i depends only on the index of the boundary step, not on how many steps or how much context the sending job accumulated, so the "reconstruct the context the previous worker had built up" story has no counterpart in the object. (iii) Most consequentially, because h enters (10) inside the time factor, the hand-off cost of a job is priced at the *sender's* skill level: splitting a high-skill job is mechanically more expensive than splitting a low-skill one. This is never flagged as an assumption, yet it is precisely what generates the counterexample in Finding 1. (iv) h_i is never measured, calibrated, bounded, or estimated anywhere in 131 pages. And Section 5's one substantive comparative static is explicitly left open — "The net effect of AI on job breadth is therefore an empirical question our framework poses rather than settles" — while Section 7 declines to test the long run at all: "The long-run margins of Section 5... operate on a horizon over which firms reorganize and workers retrain, and not enough time has passed since the AI tools became widely available for such reorganization to have worked its way into the data we observe."
why_it_matters: An eight-page section built on an unmeasured primitive, delivering no proposition, whose only comparative static is declared indeterminate and which the empirical section explicitly refuses to test, is a section a ReStud referee will ask to cut. Combined with Section 6 (see the other findings), roughly a third of the body of the paper is unfalsifiable and disconnected from the three predictions the empirics actually test — all of which come from Sections 3-4. This is the "is this one paper or several" charge in its most concrete form, and the answer as the draft stands is: one paper (short-run chaining plus its three tests) with a second, unfinished paper stapled to it.
already_addressed: The paper offers a partial defence in a footnote: "A useful reading of the hand-off cost is that it has two components: peripheral coordination work that AI can facilitate, and a remainder that rests on tacit, interpersonal, or social knowledge and is not easily executable by AI [deming2017growing]." That is an interpretation, not a measurement or a restriction on h. Appendix H mentions the long run only to justify using multi-person event logs for the *ordering* validation ("But the long-run problem of Section 5.2 is about exactly this object: a workflow partitioned into jobs, with a hand-off incurred wherever the work passes from one worker to the next"), and then never uses them for that purpose. Grep confirms no other appendix touches h_i.
fix: The paper already holds the right data and does not use it. The eight 4TU/BPI logs in Appendix H (215,715 cases, 2,048,949 events) carry an originator/resource field per event, which makes job boundaries and hand-over-of-work directly observable, case by case. Two exercises follow immediately: (a) measure the empirical distribution of hand-off points and show that boundaries fall disproportionately at low-h "natural seams" — a direct test of the paper's claim that where the firm divides matters and not merely how often; (b) recover h_i from the inter-activity waiting time at resource changes, net of the within-resource baseline, and calibrate the Section 5 trade-off on a real workflow. If neither is feasible, cut Section 5 to two pages inside Section 4 as a stated extension.

title: The discretization error bound in the proof of Proposition 4 is wrong: rounding compounds over the steps of a job, so the stated running time understates the true bound by a factor m^2, and the proposition's boundedness hypothesis is violated by the model's own primitives
location: A_omitted_proofs.tex Sec A.5 ("Proof of Proposition 4"), final paragraph; Proposition 4 statement in 6_extensions.tex
claim: The proof's entire error analysis is one sentence: "Skill and time costs accumulate additively along the manual and chaining options, so rounding the running totals down to powers of (1+epsilon) maintains a multiplicative error of at most (1+epsilon) in each coordinate. Each job's wage bill is formed by the single multiplication S*T at the point the job-closure option closes it, so it is computed to within a factor of (1+epsilon)^2. Rescaling epsilon by a constant therefore yields the claimed (1+epsilon) approximation." This is false. The table is indexed by grid values of (S, T), so every transition — R(i, S, T) -> R(i-1, S + sigma^M_i, T + m_i), and likewise the chaining transition — must re-round the new totals to grid points in order to look them up. A job containing k tasks therefore suffers k successive roundings, and the relative error in each coordinate is (1+epsilon)^k, up to (1+epsilon)^m, not (1+epsilon). "Rescaling epsilon by a constant" fixes the exponent 2 from the final multiplication; it does not fix compounding over m. The standard repair is epsilon' = Theta(epsilon/m), which multiplies the number of grid points per coordinate by m and hence the state count by m^2. The corrected bound is O(m^4 * epsilon^{-2} * log^2(mB)), whereas Proposition 4 claims O(m^2 * epsilon^{-2} * log^2(mB)). Separately, the hypothesis "whose skill, time, and hand-off costs lie in [1/B, B]" is contradicted by the model itself: Section 5.1 defines h_m = 0 ("The final job hands off to no one, so h_m = 0"), Table 2 states that "an automated step requires none" of skill, and the proof's own linking identity V(i) = R(i, 0, h_i) evaluates the table at S = 0, which is neither in the tabulated range [1/B, mB] nor a power of (1+epsilon).
why_it_matters: Proposition 4 is one of only four propositions in the paper and its content is entirely the running-time bound; if the bound is wrong the proposition as stated is false. It is also the only formal result attached to Section 5, so the long-run section's single theorem does not hold as written. This is the kind of error a theory referee at ReStud (or an EC referee, given the paper was presented at ACM EC'26) will catch on a first read, and it damages confidence in the other proofs.
already_addressed: Nothing in the paper addresses compounding. The proof does carefully bound the *ranges* to be tabulated ("a job's total skill lies in [1/B, mB], and its total time is at most 2mB^3") and correctly counts O(eps^{-1} log(mB)) grid points per coordinate, so the state-counting half of the argument is sound. It is only the error-propagation half that fails, and the h_m = 0 / zero-skill-automation violations of the boundedness hypothesis are not mentioned anywhere.
fix: Restate Proposition 4 with the corrected exponent, or give a genuine argument that compounding does not occur — for instance by rounding the *per-task* increments once rather than the running totals, and showing the resulting totals are within (1+epsilon) of the true totals by additivity, which does work and preserves the O(m^2) bound. Also weaken the hypothesis to cover zero skill costs and h_m = 0 (e.g. bound only the non-zero primitives, and handle S = 0 as a separate table entry), and state explicitly that the tabulated time range already accounts for chain times a_r / prod(q), which can exceed B.

title: Propositions 3 and 4 are computer-science results with no economic content, they are never used, and the hardness that motivates the approximation is asserted rather than established
location: 6_extensions.tex Sec 6.2 ("Computing the Firm's Optimum"), including the closing paragraph
claim: The motivation is: "The firm cannot solve its optimization problem step by step, then, and must instead consider all feasible arrangements, of which there are exponentially many." An exponential number of candidate arrangements is not a hardness statement — it is true of every interval-partition problem, most of which are polynomial, as Proposition 3 itself demonstrates. Grep confirms the words "NP-hard" and "NP-complete" appear nowhere in the paper. So the reader cannot tell why Proposition 4 must settle for (1+epsilon) rather than exactness: the stated reason is that "Skill and time costs are continuous, so the recursion must distinguish between infinitely many situations," but a continuous state space is not itself an obstruction (a DP over the Pareto frontier of reachable (skill, time) pairs is exact, and the question is whether that frontier can be super-polynomially large — which is never asked). Nor does the (1+epsilon) loss carry any economic interpretation: nothing in the model makes the firm computationally constrained, no behavioural implication is drawn from tractability, and no result elsewhere in the paper depends on either proposition. The paper concedes the algorithms are unused: "Paired with detailed measurement of the time and skill content of individual tasks, the algorithms above could be run on real workflows to ask how a given advance in AI capability would redraw them."
why_it_matters: Section 6.2 occupies a body section of a general-interest economics paper and contributes nothing an economics reader can use. Proposition 3 is a textbook O(m^2) interval DP; Proposition 4 is a standard geometric-rounding FPTAS. At ReStud this reads as material that belongs in the EC version of the paper, and — coming immediately after Section 6.1, whose value is also in doubt — it makes Section 6 as a whole look like a bolt-on. It also invites the sharper question of whether the paper's theoretical contribution is deep or mechanical, since the two most formal-looking results in the paper are the two with the least economic content.
already_addressed: Section 6's own preamble concedes the status of this material: "This section briefly provides two additional results that the framework delivers, but defers their detailed discussion to the appendix." That is an admission that neither subsection is load-bearing, not a defence of including them in the body.
fix: Move both propositions to Appendix A as a short computational note. If they are to stay in the body, they need economic content: prove NP-hardness of the long-run problem (which would give a real "chaining makes organizational design genuinely hard" message, and a reason for the approximation), and then actually run the algorithm on the O*NET workflows the paper has already constructed to produce a counterfactual — how the optimal job design of, say, the median occupation redraws as alpha rises. That would simultaneously give Section 5 the empirical content it currently lacks.

title: Section 6.1's own summary of the aggregation result argues that the paper's mechanism is macro-irrelevant, and the CES is derived holding fixed the very objects the promised comparative static moves
location: 6_extensions.tex Sec 6.1, final two paragraphs; B_macro_production.tex Sec B.1 ("Suppose the firm solves the long-run cost minimization problem (7) for a given AI quality level alpha, and obtains the optimal AI strategy T and job design J"; "Since the AI strategy and job design are fixed...")
claim: Section 6.1 concludes: "The organizational content carries over as well, but only in the parameters. That is, two economies whose production steps are identically exposed to AI, differing only in how those steps are arranged within workflows, reach the same functional form expressed by (10) but with different weights and input requirements while looking alike on any step-level exposure measure." Read plainly, this says that the paper's entire contribution — the arrangement of steps in a workflow — is invisible in the aggregate except as unidentified CES parameters. That is an argument for ignoring chaining at the macro level, not for taking it seriously. The paper then claims: "the implications people draw from improving AI quality in a CES economy carry over intact." This does not follow from Appendix B. The whole micro-to-Leontief step is executed at a *fixed* T and J chosen at a *given* alpha, so T_A, T_M, the exit threshold u, the weights theta_A, theta_M, and the required density phi are all functions of alpha. When alpha rises the firm re-chains — which is the paper's central point — and every parameter of (10) moves. A comparative static in alpha performed inside (10) with fixed parameters is therefore exactly the exercise the paper spends Sections 3-4 arguing is wrong.
why_it_matters: The paper's pitch against the task-based literature is that "linear aggregation obscures the crucial role of task interdependence" (2_literature.tex). Appendix B then produces the standard CES aggregate and Section 6.1 says the organizational content shows up only in parameters that no step-level exposure measure can distinguish. A referee will ask the obvious question: if the chaining structure is observationally equivalent to a reparameterized CES at the macro level, what is the macro payoff of the theory, and why is the aggregation in the paper at all? As written, Section 6.1 weakens the paper's own thesis.
already_addressed: The paper anticipates the question one step and answers it: "This is why workflow-level objects such as the fragmentation index have to be measured where the arrangement of work is still visible, which is what our empirical exercise in Section 7 does." That is a fair response to the measurement point but not to the substantive one: it concedes that the mechanism has no aggregate signature. Nothing anywhere addresses the fixed-T-and-J problem with the alpha comparative static.
fix: Either derive the mapping from workflow structure to the CES parameters explicitly — show how theta_A, theta_M and rho depend on the fragmentation index, so that two economies with the same step-level exposure but different fragmentation have measurably different aggregate elasticities, which would turn a liability into the paper's best macro result — or cut Section 6.1 and Appendix B and remove the CES claim from the abstract. The middle course currently taken (assert the aggregation, then concede it erases the mechanism) is the worst of the three.
